in.other_title: Debater strength (Elo) vs judge accuracy and correct-answer advantage in debate
in.rationale: Khan et al. report that the Elo advantage of being assigned the correct answer increases with aggregate Elo across 20 debaters judged by GPT-4-Turbo on QuALITY. Kenton et al. find a positive correct-answer Elo advantage for every debater but no clear trend of it growing with aggregate Elo, using 1-turn debates, different debater models and a Gemini Pro 1.5 judge across extractive and closed tasks.

out.other_title: Does debate's honesty assumption hold beyond fact-checkable claims; can humans judge?
out.rationale: Leike et al. ask whether debate's assumption that truth is easier than lying holds outside easily fact-checkable domains. Khan et al. report debaters get higher Elo when assigned the correct answer and that this advantage grows with aggregate Elo across 20 debaters; however QuALITY debates use a quote tool, so claims are fact-checkable against the text, which is the case Leike et al. exclude.
out.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether telling the truth is easier than lying in debate, for LLM debaters on QuALITY with LLM judges and a quote verification tool

open_obligations: Note that the quote tool lets debaters verify claims, which may be what makes lying hard.

out.other_title: Central claim of debate: it is harder to lie than to refute a lie
out.rationale: Irving et al. state debate rests on the empirical claim that lying is harder than refuting a lie. Khan et al. report debaters earn higher Elo when assigned the correct answer and that the advantage grows with aggregate Elo, which they read as truth-telling being easier than lying in QuALITY debates; the evidence is specific to a quote-verified reading comprehension setting.
out.scope: proposed SUPPORTS: whether it is harder to lie than to refute a lie, in QuALITY debates with LLM debaters and judges and a quote verification tool

text: In a cross-play tournament of 20 LLM debaters judged by GPT-4-Turbo, the paper reports that models obtain higher Elo when assigned the correct answer and that this advantage increases with aggregate Elo, which the authors read as telling the truth being easier than lying in QuALITY debates (a central assumption of Irving et al.). They report this holds across judges, that base LLM is the strongest indicator of persuasiveness (GPT-4-Turbo highest), and that critique-and-refinement yields less persuasive models than best-of-N.
title: Arguing the correct answer is easier, and the advantage grows with debater persuasiveness
